title: The Young Women Quietly Converting to Catholicism
author: Georgina Mumford
content:
![The Young Women Quietly Converting to
Catholicism](https://storage.ghost.io/c/65/af/65afbdb5-30bf-4286-acc4-9535069adb42/content/images/2026/08/AP424809377337.jpg)

If you've read about Christianity's apparent revival, you have likely come
across its familiar protagonist: the young male convert, often cast as the
poster boy for Gen Z's crisis of meaning, or else a fervent culture warrior
dreaming of a restored Christendom. But amid the slew of opinion pieces
attempting to explain why he and his friends are supposedly filling out pews,
a central question remains unanswered: Where are the women?

A recent Gallup poll suggests that women, long the more religious sex, are
losing interest in faith. Between 2024 and 2025, 42 percent of American men
aged eighteen to twenty-nine said religion was "very important" in their
lives, up fourteen percentage points in just two years. At 29 percent, their
female counterparts sat considerably lower. Polling also suggests young women
now [_leave_](https://www.americansurveycenter.org/newsletter/young-women-are-
leaving-church-in-unprecedented-numbers/?ref=compactmag.com) religious
communities at higher rates than young men, in a reversal of a longstanding
pattern.

My Catholic church in Northwest London is full of faithful grandmas, mothers,
and little girls darting in and out of the side chapels during Mass. But the
young adult presence at the parish undoubtedly skews male. While some dioceses
have reported conversion stats to the contrary in recent years, with Gen Z
women leading the charge, I seldom meet Catholic women my age who weren't
raised in the faith. Certainly, I haven't seen their experiences debated in
the news to the extent that my newly Christian male friends' had been. Thus,
the hunt for the elusive female convert began.
